# Machine learning

Models small enough to train inside a box, in plain Kotlin, while you watch. Flow matching carries one 2D or 3D point cloud onto another and hands back the deformation between them; the multi-output regression head it trains is usable on its own. See [Flow Matching](../flow_matching.md).

## deepsets.kt { #deepsets-kt }

A learned two-body interaction: the acceleration on a particle as a function of the neighbours
around it, fitted by autodiff from examples of any rule that can already be evaluated.

`flowMatch` learns `v(x, t)`: where a particle should go given only where it is. That can carry
a cloud onto a shape, and it is blind to the other particles. An interaction is the other kind
of rule:

    a_i = phi( v_i, SUM_j psi(x_j - x_i, v_j - v_i), MEAN_j psi(...) )

two small networks and a reduction over neighbours. This is the Deep Sets form, and its
aggregation is permutation-invariant over any number of neighbours, so one set of weights works
for a particle with three neighbours and a particle with three hundred. Classical boids is *one
particular choice* of `psi` and `phi`, so the family contains it.

### Why both a sum and a mean

Reynolds separation is a **sum**: being crowded by twenty neighbours pushes harder than being
crowded by two. Alignment and cohesion are **means**, since they are averages of neighbour
velocity and position. A mean-only aggregator cannot represent separation at any width, and a
sum-only one makes alignment scale with crowding, so `phi` is fed both, at a cost of
`messageWidth` extra inputs. `DeepSetsWeights.sumScale` keeps the summed branch in a sane range.

### The feature map is where the physics goes

`psi` is not fed the raw offset. It is fed `interactionFeatures`: the offset and velocity
difference, plus the **unit direction scaled by a small radial basis**, `u*p` and `u*p^2`, where
`p` is a bounded proximity that rises as neighbours get close.

Separation goes as `1/r` over a four-hundred-fold range of `r`, and a `tanh` network cannot
form the *product* of a direction and a steep radial profile out of Cartesian components at any
practical width. Alignment and cohesion are plain means, and linear in the inputs, so they
survive the raw encoding. Measured by ablation against the flocking rule: fed raw Cartesian
offsets the model reproduces those two to a relative error of **0.036** and separation only to
**0.78**, which is barely better than predicting the average.

A radial interaction is a direction times a profile, so handing the network `u` already
multiplied by a couple of profile terms states the *form* of a two-body law rather than
transcribing boids. The profile's coefficients, the velocity dependence, and how the summed and
meaned branches combine are all still learned.

### Trained by [`afield.stdlib.ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape), not by Smile

Smile's MLP cannot express this: the gradient has to flow back through a sum over a
*variable-length* neighbour set, and `psi` is applied once per neighbour with shared weights.
`autodiff.kt` is reverse-mode over a tape, which handles it without knowing anything about
networks, since the tape records whatever the forward pass did. Cost is one forward and one
backward sweep per batch whatever the neighbour counts are.

### The weights come out as [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights)

Both halves are packaged in the same flat layout the flow-matching work already uses, so
`MlpWeights.glsl` emits them for the GPU unchanged and the parity machinery in
`four.neural-field-parity.smoke` applies to them without modification.

[`EquivariantWeights`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt-equivariantweights) is the same model constrained so that rotating a neighbourhood rotates the answer with it.

### EquivariantWeights { #deepsets-kt-equivariantweights }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">EquivariantWeights</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">psi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">channels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">velocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">accelScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sumScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/deepsets/#L514)

## flowmatching.kt { #flowmatching-kt }

Flow matching over 2D and 3D point clouds — `flowMatch` trains a velocity field that carries one
distribution onto another, and the field it returns can be sampled, integrated part-way, or drawn.

The idea is small enough to state completely. Pick a point `x0` from where you are starting and a
point `x1` from where you want to end up, and declare that the straight line between them is the
path a particle should take: at time `t` it is at `xt = (1-t)·x0 + t·x1`, travelling at `x1 - x0`.
Now fit a network `v(x, t)` to that velocity by least squares over many random `(x0, x1, t)`
triples. No two straight lines agree where they cross, so the fit cannot reproduce any single one
of them; what it converges to is the *average* velocity through each point at each time, and
integrating that average from `t = 0` to `t = 1` transports the whole starting distribution onto
the whole target one. That is the entire trick, and it is why there is no adversary, no sampler in
the training loop, and nothing to diverge — the loss is a plain regression MSE.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val target = flowSamples(myLine, 600, jitter = 4.0)   // sampled FLine + noise
val field = flowMatch(target, options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000))
val cloud = field.sample(600)                         // fresh points from the same shape
val threads = field.paths(80)                         // the trajectories, as FLines
```

With a `from` cloud supplied it becomes a morph instead of a generator, and then `FlowMatchField.transport`
is the interesting call: it runs the ODE only part-way, so `transport(a, to = 0.5)` is a genuine
half-way shape rather than a vertex-wise average of two point lists.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val morph = flowMatch(to = flowSamples(lineB, 600), from = flowSamples(lineA, 600))
val halfway = morph.transport(flowSamples(lineA, 600), to = 0.5)
```

### Coordinates

Training happens in a normalised frame — the target cloud (both clouds, for a morph) is centred
and isotropically scaled to roughly unit variance — because a Gaussian source has to be
commensurate with the data for any of this to work, and FLine coordinates are usually in the
hundreds. The scaling is a single factor rather than per-axis, so it cannot squash a shape's aspect
ratio. [`FlowMatchField`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt-flowmatchfield) converts at its boundary, so everything you pass in and get back is in the
coordinates you started with.

2D and 3D are distinguished by the data, not by a flag: a cloud whose `z` never varies is trained
as a 2D problem and its points come back on that same `z` plane. Pass `FlowMatchOptions.dimension`
to override. It matters — a 2D shape trained as 3D gets a Gaussian's worth of spread in `z` that
the field then has to learn to collapse.

### What this is not

- **Not a big model.** The default is two hidden layers of 64 `leaky` units trained by RMSProp,
  which is right for a few thousand points in two or three dimensions and nothing like enough for
  images. Training is single-threaded and per-sample (Smile's MLP has no batched matmul), so cost
  scales with `steps × batch`; see the timings in `FlowMatchingTest`.
- **Not able to change topology.** Integrating a velocity field is a continuous invertible map, so
  it cannot tear a loop open or join two strands into one — a flow can only deform. With
  `FlowCoupling.PAIRED` this stops being an abstraction and starts being the dominant error term:
  asking a straight segment to become a closed ring makes the mean landing error fifteen times
  worse than asking a small circle to do it, because the two ends of the segment are pulled to the
  same place and their paths have to cross. Give a closed target a closed source.
- **Not exact.** The field is an average over crossing paths, so samples land *near* the target
  distribution, not on it. Sharp corners smooth off, and thin structure needs more `steps` and more
  `hidden` before it resolves. `FlowMatchField.loss` is the training MSE, which measures the velocity
  fit and not the quality of the samples — judge those by looking, or with `chamferDistance`.
- **Not ordered.** `FlowMatchField.sample` returns an unordered cloud. Recovering an FLine from it is a
  separate problem; `FlowMatchField.transport` sidesteps it by moving points you already have, which
  keeps whatever order they came in.
- **Not conditional.** There is no class label or text prompt input — one field carries one
  distribution onto one other.

## neuralparticles.kt { #neuralparticles-kt }

Taking a small trained network to the GPU: [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights) is a flat, layer-major snapshot of a
multilayer perceptron's weights, and `MlpWeights.glsl` emits a GLSL function that evaluates the
same network out of a storage buffer.

What that buys is a particle whose update rule was *trained* rather than written. `flowMatch`
(see `flowmatching.kt`) already fits a velocity field `v(x, t)` in a couple of seconds of pure
Kotlin; a compute shader stepping a buffer of particles can evaluate that field per particle per
frame, provided the two sides agree about what the network *is*. This file is that agreement,
and `afield.examples.four.NeuralFieldParitySmoke` measures that it holds on real hardware.

Nothing here is particle-specific: a net that takes a position and returns a velocity, a net
that takes a neighbour offset and returns an interaction term, and a net that takes anything and
returns anything are all the same object. The particle system is what consumes it.

### Two comparisons, not one

There are two distinct errors between "the network Smile trained" and "the network the GPU
runs", they have very different sizes, and conflating them makes the unavoidable one look like
a bug.

- **Precision.** Smile evaluates in `Double`; a shader evaluates in `float`. Agreement is
  therefore limited to fp32 by construction — a few parts in a million, relative, and rather
  more for an output that is a cancelling sum. `MlpWeights.evaluate` is the fp32 reference *in
  Kotlin*, so this error can be measured on its own with no GPU present at all.
- **Transcription.** The order of the layers, the orientation of each weight matrix, the slope
  of the leaky ReLU, whether the output layer has an activation. Every one of these is either
  exactly right or grossly wrong, and a grossly wrong one still produces smooth, plausible,
  entirely fictional output.

So the GPU is compared against `MlpWeights.evaluate`, fp32 against fp32, where the only
remaining freedom is the order the hardware chooses to accumulate a dot product in; and
`evaluate` is compared against Smile separately. A single comparison against `Double` would
have to be loose enough to absorb the precision gap, which is a tolerance wide enough to hide a
transposed matrix in a small network.

### The weight layout

`MlpWeights.flat` runs layer by layer from the first hidden layer to the output layer. Each
layer contributes its weight matrix, row-major with one row per *output* neuron, then its bias
vector. So for a layer with `n` outputs over `p` inputs, the weight from input `i` to output `o`
is at `weightOffset(layer) + o * p + i`, and its bias is at `biasOffset(layer) + o`. The input
layer contributes nothing — it holds no weights.

This is the layout a shader wants to read, and it is also the layout Smile happens to store.
The two are not relied on to coincide: `VectorMLP.exportWeights` in `flowmatching.kt` reads
element by element through `DenseMatrix.get(row, column)` rather than copying memory, so a
change of storage order upstream cannot silently transpose the network.

## neuralparticles_system.kt { #neuralparticles-system-kt }

A particle system driven by a trained velocity field: [`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) integrates a
buffer of particles along the field in a compute pass and draws the same allocation as points,
with no copy between the two.

`neuralparticles.kt` settles what a network *is* on both sides of the CPU/GPU line and emits
the GLSL that evaluates one; this file is what consumes that GLSL. The chain from a target
shape to a moving cloud is `flowMatch`, then `FlowMatchField.export()`, then
[`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) and `installInto`. `afield.examples.four.NeuralParticlesSmoke` is the
GPU smoke over that whole path, and the `neural_particles` agent transcript is that chain as
three boxes.

Two of the design decisions reach the caller, so they are stated here rather than only on the
declarations that implement them:

- **Positions are stored in the training frame**, not in the coordinates the field was
  authored in, because integrating in input coordinates would convert into the frame and back
  out again on every step to reach the same answer. So [`NeuralParticleSettings`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-neuralparticlesettings)'s `viewScale`
  and `viewCenter` are in normalised units, where a scale of about 2.6 frames a cloud of
  roughly unit variance.
- **A particle is travelling a journey, not wandering a force field.** A flow is a map: each
  particle goes from one specific source point to wherever the field takes it by `t = 1`, then
  starts again. That is why it carries a `start` and a `t`, and why `reset` has to seed from
  the field's own source cloud whenever the field has one.

Which settings are live follows from where each one is read. `particleCount` sizes the particle
buffer, the compute dispatch and the point mesh at construction, so it cannot be raised
afterwards, and `name` is written into the module and buffer names there. `phaseSpread`,
`sourceJitter` and `randomSeed` are read by `reset`, which fills the buffer, so changing one
takes a `reset` call. Everything else is read through a push-constant lambda every frame and
takes effect on the next one, including `stepsPerCycle` and `dwellCycles`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/neuralparticles_system.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/neuralparticles_system/)

**Used in:** [Neural particle systems](../neural_particles.md)
